**The Imjin War (1592–1598)** – also known as the Japanese invasions of Korea – was a major conflict between the Japanese forces of Toyotomi Hideyoshi and the Korean Joseon dynasty, with Chinese Ming dynasty support. | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **Timeframe** | 1592–1598 | | **Key Players** | • **Japan** – led by Toyotomi Hideyoshi, aiming to conquer Korea and then China.
• **Korea (Joseon)** – defended by King Seonjo, with the help of the Korean navy under Admiral Yi Sun-sin.
• **China (Ming)** – intervened to protect the Ming dynasty’s interests and to stop Japanese expansion. | | **Causes** | • Hideyoshi’s ambition to unify East Asia under Japanese rule.
• Korea’s strategic position as a gateway to China.
• Economic motives: control over trade routes and resources. | | **Major Phases** | 1. **Initial Invasion (1592)** – Japanese forces landed at Busan, quickly captured Seoul, and advanced northward.
2. **Korean & Ming Counterattack (1593–1595)** – Korean navy’s naval victories (notably the Battle of Myeongnyang) and Ming land forces pushed back the Japanese.
3. **Second Invasion (1597–1598)** – Japanese attempted to regain lost territory; ultimately failed due to logistical issues and continued resistance. | | **Key Battles** | • **Battle of Hansan Island** (1592) – Yi Sun-sin’s naval victory using turtle ships.
• **Battle of Myeongnyang** (1597) – Yi Sun-sin’s 13‑ship fleet defeated 133 Japanese ships with only 12 vessels.
• **Siege of Ulsan** (1598) – Japanese stronghold captured by Ming forces. | | **Outcome** | • Japan suffered heavy casualties and logistical losses; the war ended with the withdrawal of Japanese forces.
• Korea remained independent but devastated; the war exposed weaknesses in Joseon’s military and administrative systems.
• China’s involvement solidified its role as a regional power but strained its resources. | | **Legacy** | • The war is celebrated in Korea for the heroic defense led by Admiral Yi Sun-sin, whose tactics are studied in naval warfare.
